_purpose: Every source considered for a numeric input to this project's cost model, with verification status. This file is the methodology-transparency exhibit required by the project brief. Read-only research record; not derived from either source project.

usable_sources.citation: Alahmadi, B., Axon, L., Martinovic, I. "99% False Positives: A Qualitative Study of SOC Analysts' Perspectives on Security Alarms." USENIX Security Symposium, 2022.
usable_sources.methodology: n=20 survey respondents, n=21 semi-structured interviews. IRB-approved. Academic funding (University of Oxford).
usable_sources.mandatory_caveat: The '99%' figure in the paper's own title is ONE analyst's verbal estimate given in an interview, not a measured rate across the sample. The paper itself states that analysts use the term 'false positive' inconsistently, which the authors flag as a reason the number is likely unreliable as a general statistic. This project never cites '99%' as a measured false-positive rate; it is cited only as an example of how unreliable self-reported FP-rate language is in this literature.
usable_sources.usable_for: narrative context on how analysts talk about alert volume; NOT as a cost or rate figure

usable_sources.citation: Sundaramurthy, S.C., et al. "A Human Capital Model for Mitigating Security Analyst Burnout." USENIX SOUPS (Symposium On Usable Privacy and Security), 2015.
usable_sources.methodology: Six-month embedded fieldwork inside one SOC, approximately 26 analysts.
usable_sources.mandatory_caveat: Contains NO minutes-per-alert figure and NO dollar figure anywhere in the paper. It documents the burnout mechanism (analysts leaving the tier-1 role due to alert-volume fatigue) qualitatively.
usable_sources.usable_for: narrative context on why alert volume matters to a SOC as an organization, not as a numeric input

rejected_sources.citation: Ponemon Institute / Devo. "The 2019 State of SOC Report." (n=554, sponsored study.)
rejected_sources.why_rejected: Full text checked. Methodology is disclosed (n=554, survey), but the report contains NO minutes-per-alert figure anywhere in its text. Any secondary source (blog, vendor whitepaper) citing this report for a minutes-per-alert number is citing a number the source document does not contain.

rejected_sources.citation: Various AI-SOC vendor blog posts citing '25 minutes per alert' or '30-70 minutes per alert'.
rejected_sources.why_rejected: No disclosed methodology, no disclosed sample, no traceable primary citation for the number in any post checked. Most of these posts are published by vendors selling a product that replaces the manual triage process whose cost they are quoting, which is a direct incentive to inflate the baseline they are replacing.

unverifiable_claims.claim: Sandia National Laboratories published alert-fatigue research.
unverifiable_claims.status: COULD NOT BE VERIFIED. A prior research pass searched for this citation four separate ways and could not locate a real, traceable Sandia publication matching the claim. It is recorded here explicitly as an unverified claim, not cited as a source, and not used anywhere in this project's numbers or narrative.
